1. Executive summary

Recommendation (conditional). For the ground conditions assumed as the base case (G1/G2: allowable bearing ≥ 150 kPa, no expansive clay, no shallow water), support the Option B trusses on the hybrid stability system S3: 22 UC 305×305×97 side columns with fixed bases about the strong axis, propped at the eaves by two 5.4 m-deep roof-plane wind girders that span between braced gables; gable wind posts with designed minor-axis restraint; end-bay roof girders and bottom-chord ties; and longitudinal wall bracing in bays 1 and 5. Found the columns on reinforced pads cast integral with a continuous reinforced strip under the masonry walls (F2). Estimated supporting-system cost: USD 421k (P50), P10–P90 389k–457k; deterministic central estimate 399k. The margin over the braced system S1 is small: 2.0% at central rates, and S3 is cheaper than S1 in 67% of trials and cheaper than S2 in 89%. If the site investigation finds poor or wet ground (G3), the braced system S1 with pinned bases becomes the cheaper and simpler choice (USD 452k against 456k). The stability system should therefore be confirmed after the site investigation (gate G-B).

Answers to the ten questions

  1. Is the existing side-column arrangement suitable? No. With a complete bracing system, the modelled UC 254×254×73 columns on pinned 4 × M24 bases deflect ≈80–100 mm under the central wind (qp 0.85 kPa). The limit for the 12.23 m masonry is h/300 = 40.8 mm. The section also fails strength (utilisation ≈1.1) at 1.20 kPa. In addition, two east-gable columns have no footing, there are no gable wind posts, the roof bracing is four 20 mm rods, and the north wall over the loggia has no transfer structure. The grid itself (11 lines @ 5.56 m, columns within the 420 mm wall/pier zone) is suitable and is retained.
  2. Sections and restraint. S3: UC 305×305×97 (regional stock, by study judgement; 308 mm deep), fixed base about the strong axis, propped at the eaves. Utilisation 0.609; 0.931 with no masonry restraint over the full 13.08 m. Transverse deflection 26.1 mm and longitudinal eaves sway 40.7 mm against 40.8 mm. S1 needs UC 305×305×137 (pinned) and S2 needs UC 356×368×153 (imported, by study judgement). The UB alternatives no longer pass once the purlins are not relied on as girder chords, and in any case they depend on masonry restraint.
  3. Braced, moment or hybrid? Hybrid on firm ground, braced on poor ground. S2 is the most expensive in every soil scenario (5% above S3 at G2) and is not recommended. The gap between S3 and S1 (8k) is within the estimating uncertainty, so non-cost factors also count. S3 is self-stable during erection, has transverse stiffness reserve and uses the lightest columns. S1 has simpler pinned bases and smaller pads, which win where the ground is poor.
  4. Can the gallery or integrated framing help? Not in the recommended scheme. The gallery reaches only +7.85 m, has no designed foundations and carries placeholder sections. The stair cores (walls to +10.80 m, construction unverified, no footings) could replace the east-gable bracing and the bay-5 wall bracing if they are proven to be RC shear walls. That is a conditional optimisation estimated at USD 10–15k, not a basis for design. The single-storey office wing should remain structurally independent.
  5. Most economical credible foundation. F2, reinforced pads cast integral with a 0.60 × 0.45 m reinforced wall strip, is the cheapest arrangement for every system in every soil scenario. The wall weight is counted only where the wall actually exists: net of doors, the north loggia and the east glazed slot. For S3 the pads are 2.3–3.3 m square and 0.80 m deep (the depth is set by the holding-down anchorage). Under G3, F3 (deep pads with ground beams over void formers) costs only about USD 1,136 more and is the prudent choice if the clay is expansive.
  6. Governing foundation actions. Uplift and overturning under the concurrent ULS combinations govern, not bearing. Braced-bay columns see ≈309 kN uplift and the braced gable posts ≈420 kN. The S3 fixed bases carry ≈200–220 kNm together with up to ≈290 kN of uplift. Ordinary truss bearings deliver 55–92 kN uplift (qp 0.85–1.20). The construction stage, before the masonry is built, governs several pads.
  7. Quantities (S1 / S2 / S3). Supporting steel 84 / 79 / 74 t. Foundation concrete 190 / 182 / 229 m³. Reinforcement, including anchor reinforcement, 6.1 / 8.1 / 8.9 t. Excavation 649 / 626 / 746 m³ (§13).
  8. Costs (central, G2/F2). USD 406,705 / 420,305 / 398,792. P50 429k / 441k / 421k. VAT and the common Option B roof package (≈USD 195k, R2) are excluded. S3 has the least steel and the most concrete.
  9. Most robust. On firm ground, S3: it keeps its stiffness reserve transversely and is self-stable in erection. Selected-design sensitivity failures: S1 SLS wind at 1.20 kPa, Dominant opening cpi +0.55, Dominant opening in suction zone, cpi -1.08 (factored 1.3); S2 SLS wind at 1.20 kPa, Base fixity: rotational spring 50 MNm/rad (G2), Base fixity: rotational spring 20 MNm/rad (G3); S3 SLS wind at 1.20 kPa (§15). On poor or wet ground, S1. Two assumptions can reverse the choice: the ground (G3 favours S1) and the wall construction (lightweight cladding removes the masonry stiffness criterion; §15).
  10. Information needed before detailed design. Confirmation of the wall construction; the Harare design wind speed and the governing code set; a site investigation (trial pits, DPSH/boreholes, swell and collapse tests, groundwater, subgrade modulus for base fixity); equipment and rigging weights; supplier prices for UC 305, CHS and holding-down assemblies; and the construction sequence (§18).
Option B issues reported, not redesigned. (a) When the gable trusses act as lateral-system collectors, their 2L80×8 top chords reach axial utilisation ≈0.8–0.9 before purlin bending, against 0.72 in R2. Consider 2L90×8, as on the interior lines. (b) The gable bottom-chord heel panels need out-of-plane restraint under uplift (elastic critical factor 0.22 without it). The eigen-analysis also shows the gable bottom chord between ties at α ≈ 2.0, which is a truss-member check for the Option B design. (c) The truss bearing as modelled is 145 mm eccentric to the column axis. (d) The 3D truss reactions are 10–25% above R2's 2D screening values (Table 3.2). (e) The bearing bolts act as ties in wind and should be preloaded (slip-resistant) or fitted, not ordinary bolts in slotted holes.

2. Project description and study scope

The auditorium is a 55.9 × 33.0 m hall. Eleven Option B trusses span 32.4 m between side-wall columns at 5.56 m centres (grid lines 0–10, x = 3.25–58.85 m). The stage is at the west end (line 0), and the gallery and stair cores are at the east (x 36.6–58.7 m). A single-storey office wing (+4.42 m) adjoins the west gable. The side walls are 300 mm masonry infill between the columns, 12.5 m high, with clerestory windows at +10.10 to +11.80 m in bays 0–6 and doors in bays 0, 4, 7 and 9. A 9.5 m loggia opening on the north side (x 43–52.5 m) rises to +4.00 m.

Scope: roof support columns, side-wall and gable framing, longitudinal and transverse stability, roof-plane girders and bracing, bottom-chord restraint, truss-to-column and base connections, foundations and ground beams, and the interfaces with the gallery, entrances, cores and office wing. Excluded: the detached children's church, other standalone buildings, the Option B truss configuration (fixed), and the gallery, core and office structures (interfaces only). The study did not modify southgate.ifc or the original design project. All analysis used isolated study models.

2.1 Method

  1. Read-only audit of the authoritative IFC (sha256 verified against bim/publish_record.json) and the migration audit reports.
  2. An independent 3D frame model (scripts/model_b.py, frame3d.py) of all 11 Option B trusses (R2 member sizes), 22 columns, 12 gable posts and every bracing system. Solver verified against closed-form results (Appendix A).
  3. Characteristic load cases with SANS 10160-1 combinations. Eight wind cases (four directions, two internal pressures) at qp 0.85 and 1.20 kPa.
  4. For each stability system, a sweep over 6–9 column sections. In each run the girders, bracing and posts are re-sized for strength and then stiffened until the SLS limits are met.
  5. Pad design for every base: three soil scenarios × three arrangements. Bearing, uplift, overturning, sliding, bending, shear and punching are checked, and anchor embedment is coupled to pad depth.
  6. Line-item costing (quantity × rate × factor), Monte Carlo on correlated rate groups, and sensitivity re-runs of the sizing.

3. Recommended roof-truss design basis

Option B is the fixed basis: a duo-pitch Warren truss with verticals, 12 panels @ 2.70 m, span 32.40 m (bearings at y = 0.30 / 32.70 m), 15° pitch, top chord +12.38 m at the heel and +16.72 m at the ridge, bottom chord +10.90 m, heel depth 1.48 m, ridge depth 5.82 m, 11 trusses @ 5.56 m, ≈42.1 t. The geometry was verified against the IFC truss assemblies (bounding boxes x = 3.12…58.98, z = 10.67…16.77 m). Member sizes follow the R2 central run: TC 2L90×8 (gables 2L80×8), BC 2L80×8, end diagonals 2L100×8, other diagonals 2L75×6, verticals 2L60/2L75×6, king post 2L100×8, end posts 2L70×6. The truss was not re-optimised.

3.1 Bearing condition

The trusses bear at the top-chord heel on column cap plates at +12.28/+12.38 m. In S1 and S3 both bearings are pinned (bolts finally tightened after the roof dead load is applied), so the roof props both column heads. Option B's gravity spread is only 1–2 mm, so the resulting thrust is small (it is included in the analysis). In S2 the bottom chord is also connected to the column at +10.90 m (a 1.48 m “knee”), which makes each truss line a portal. The R2 bearing seat does not provide moment continuity, so S2 needs a purpose-designed heel connection.

5. Structural loading and design assumptions

5.1 Design standards

No Zimbabwean loading or steel design standard could be confirmed from published sources. Statutory Instrument 41 of 1978 references a Standards Association of Zimbabwe concrete code, and the Model Building By-laws govern approvals, but neither sets wind or steel design rules found in this review. Consistent with R2 and regional practice, the study uses SANS 10160-1/-2/-3 (actions), SANS 10162-1:2011 (steel, limit states, φ 0.9, n = 1.34), SANS 10100-1 (concrete, BS 8110 basis) and EN 1992-4 (anchorage, by analogy), with EN 1991-1-4 informative pressure coefficients. These are suitable for the next design stage only if the appointed ECZ-registered engineer and Harare City Council accept them. Edition and consequence class must be confirmed: CC2 is recommended for a 2,000-seat assembly building (reliability class RC2 minimum; consider RC3 for the roof given the occupancy).

5.3 Combinations and criteria

  • ULS: 1.35G; 1.2G + 1.6Qr; 1.2G + 1.6Qrig; 1.2G + 1.3W; 0.9G + 1.3W (equipment excluded where favourable), each with notional loads.
  • SLS: 1.0W at the characteristic central pressure qp 0.85 kPa. Masonry cracking is a serviceability state, so the central basis is used, and 1.20 kPa is a sensitivity case. Limit h/300 = 40.8 mm, with h = 12.23 m of masonry (FFL to wall head), for column deflection and longitudinal eaves sway, because the masonry infill spans to the columns. R2 used h/150, which suits lightweight cladding only. Posts: L/300 relative to the chord.
  • Foundations: allowable bearing under characteristic combinations (Meyerhof effective area); uplift, overturning and sliding under EQU factors (0.9 on permanent stabilising); construction stage with walls absent at 0.75 × W(1.20 kPa) (assumed reduced exposure period).
  • Second order: αcr = (H/V)(h/δ) per frame line and wall line; first-order analysis is acceptable if αcr ≥ 10. An elastic eigen-analysis was used to find member-level modes.

7. Lateral stability alternatives

All three systems share the longitudinal system, because longitudinal moment frames would put the columns into minor-axis bending and are impractical. That system comprises: six gable wind posts per gable (UB 533×210×82, placed at s = 2.7, 8.1…29.7 m so as to clear the west doors and the east glazed slot); end-bay roof girders in bays 0 and 9 across the full width; end-bay cross frames and bottom-chord bracing; bottom-chord ties at 5.4 m; eaves struts; and wall bracing in bays 1 and 5 on both sides. The north wall has no bay free of clerestories or openings, so the wall bracing is an X below the sill (+9.90 m) with knee braces inside the 1.08 m window piers.

Variants considered and not adopted. (i) Cantilever columns without girders (R2): no catalogue UC meets the deflection limit. (ii) Cores as the east stability elements (S3-core): this would remove the east-gable and bay-5 bracing, but it depends on unverified RC cores that have no foundations. It is held as a conditional optimisation (§10.4). (iii) Intermediate moment frames to shorten the girders: frames stiff enough to help the girders need UC 356 columns, which costs more than the girders they replace. (iv) Masonry gables as shear walls: credible in Harare practice, but it needs reinforced masonry design and a steel erection sequence that does not depend on the masonry. Recorded as an optimisation.

8. Side-column optimisation

Each candidate was analysed with its complete system re-sized (Figure 8.1, Table 8.1). Column checks follow SANS 10162-1 cl 13.8 (cross-section, overall member and lateral-torsional buckling), with Kx = 1.0 (S1, S2) or 0.85 (S3), minor-axis and LTB restraint at 3.3 m from the masonry ties (robustness check: no restraint over the full 13.08 m), ω2 = 1.13, and the bearing eccentricity moment included. The governing case in all systems is longitudinal wind with zone-A suction on the end bays plus wall-bracing forces in the braced-bay columns.

8.1 Selection logic

A candidate must (a) pass strength and both SLS limits (transverse deflection and longitudinal sway, 40.8 mm), (b) remain adequate with no masonry restraint at all, checked over the full 13.08 m column height, and (c) fit the 420 mm wall/pier zone. Candidates deeper than 420 mm were also costed with the pier enlargement priced, and none of them passes (a) and (b). The resulting columns are UC 305×305×137 for S1, UC 356×368×153 for S2 and UC 305×305×97 for S3. Fixing the bases makes each column ≈2.4× stiffer against wall wind (wL4/185EI against 5wL4/384EI), which is why S3's column is 40 kg/m lighter than S1's. The existing UC 254×254×73 passes in S3 with masonry restraint (39.4 mm, utilisation 0.73) but fails without it (1.65). It is acceptable only if the masonry ties are designed as restraints.

Method limitation. The stiffening loop upsizes one bracing group at a time, choosing the group with the largest strain energy per tonne under the governing SLS case. It is a heuristic. The S3 UC 254×254×89 result (failing longitudinal sway while the lighter UC 254×73 passes) is a path artefact of the heuristic, not a property of the section. Costs from the sizing method are uncertain by ≈±5–10%, and this is carried into the Monte Carlo (§15).

Gable posts: UB 533×210×82 posts are adequate only with minor-axis restraint. Without it, utilisation is 2.6–4.6 over the 14–17.5 m height. All systems therefore include two rows of horizontal restraint struts per gable (CHS 88.9×3.2, ≈0.9 t), and the masonry ties must not be relied on alone.

Construction stage: S2 and S3 columns are self-stable cantilevers once grouted. S1 columns need guying until the girders and gable bracing are complete (priced as temporary works).

All bracing is CHS (S355J2H), designed for compression with both diagonals active, so that the stiffness assumed in the model is the stiffness provided. Tension-only rods would be lighter but would halve the X-panel stiffness, which the deflection limits do not allow without re-analysis. Purlins are not relied on as girder chords. In the design runs the purlins are nominal links (0.1% of their axial stiffness), so the eaves struts and inner chords carry all the girder bending. The independent review found that an earlier draft let the purlins share it.

9.1 Connection concepts (not connection designs)

  • Truss bearing (S1/S3): concentric cap plate on the column (eliminating the modelled 145 mm offset, or designing the column for Rv×0.145 ≈ 18–21 kNm). Preloaded (slip-resistant) M20 8.8 bolts, because the bearing acts as a tie for the eaves girders in wind; slotted holes only if the bolts are preloaded after the roof dead load. Heel restraint cleats at gable lines 0 and 10.
  • Knee (S2): TC heel and BC heel both bolted to the column flange. Knee forces ≈229 kN horizontal at ULS. The paired-angle BC and gussets at the heel need re-design for this force (a truss change outside this study's mandate, and a further reason S2 is not recommended).
  • Bracing ends: slotted-tube to 10–12 mm gusset, 2–4 M20 8.8 bolts, gusset welded to the column flange or the truss node plate. The wall X-bracing is made in two halves joined at a central node plate (CHS 219 cannot cross inside a 300 mm wall), placed on the inner face or in a wall chase. The lower ends connect to gussets on the column feet below FFL, inside the concrete encasement pocket.
  • Gable posts: base pinned (4 M24), head connected to the gable truss TC node through a vertically slotted bracket (horizontal restraint, vertical freedom).
  • Bases: Figure 9.1 and §11.

Figure 9.1 Pinned (S1) and fixed (S3) base and pad concept sections, indicative.

10. Foundation optimisation

10.1 Ground conditions

No geotechnical report exists for the site (project-wide search). Published Harare evidence is limited. A University of Zimbabwe study recorded intermediate- and low-plasticity clays, sodic soils and inadequate bearing in places, and recommended a minimum founding depth of 1.5 m for bearing above 100 kPa. Granite-derived residual soils in the region can be collapsible. The study therefore uses three scenarios, all assumptions:

ScenarioAllowable bearingMin. founding below FGLDensityBase frictionGroundwater / heave
G1 favourable: dense residual granite / gravelly sand200 kPa1.0 m18 kN/m³0.45none
G2 moderate (base): stiff residual sandy clay150 kPa1.2 m18 kN/m³0.35none
G3 poor: firm intermediate-plasticity clay, possibly expansive100 kPa1.5 m17 kN/m³0.30perched water at −1.40 (buoyant uplift); heave → F3

Below about 75 kPa allowable, or with high swell potential, pads and strips stop being appropriate and a raft or piles would be required. That is outside this study and is identified as the decision threshold.

10.2 Arrangements

  • F1 independent pads (no wall weight relied on) plus a lightly reinforced wall strip.
  • F2 pads cast integral with a continuous reinforced strip under the masonry. The wall weight over 3.0 m (216 kN) counts as permanent ballast. Construction stage checked with the walls absent.
  • F3 deeper pads with 0.35 × 0.75 m ground beams spanning 5.56 m that carry the wall (void formers in G3). The full bay of wall load (≈400 kN) goes into the pads.

10.3 Governing actions and R2 concept pads

Uplift and overturning under the concurrent combinations govern, not bearing. In S3 the ordinary columns need pads of about 2.3–2.4 m square, the braced-bay columns 3.1–3.3 m, and the braced gable posts about 3 m, all 0.80 m deep. The depth is set by the anchorage: 450 mm embedment plus room to anchor the hairpins below the heads. R2's 2.0×2.0×1.0 m pinned pad suits ordinary S1 bearings. Its 3.5×3.5×0.70 m fixed-base pad is of the right order only for the braced bays. The wall ballast assumed for F2 is the weight actually present over 3.0 m at each pad, net of doors, the north loggia (no wall on the strip) and the east glazed slot. Its sensitivity to a lighter masonry (0.7 × 72 kN/m) is given in §15.

10.4 Integrated framing (gallery, cores, office)

Gallery: its slabs (+4.4 to +7.85 m) could restrain columns 7–9 at mid-height, but they do not reach the eaves, so they cannot shorten the girders. Using them would add lateral load to undesigned rakers and RC columns that have no footings. Not used. Cores: their walls stop at +10.80 m, 0.10 m below the truss bottom chord, and the core end walls (6.2 m long in x) cross under trusses 10 and 11. As designed RC shear walls with foundations they could take the east transverse and longitudinal reactions. That would remove the east gable bracing and the bay-5 wall bracing (≈3–4 t, USD 10–15k) but add core reinforcement and footings. Conditional. Office wing: its +4.42 m roof deck could prop the west gable posts, reducing the post size, but only if the office frame is braced for it. Not assumed.

Figure 10.3 Foundation concept plan, recommended S3, F2, G2 (indicative).

11. Foundation reinforcement and anchorage considerations

  • Holding-down design uses concurrent actions. The tension row is designed for the worst concurrent (N, M) pair from each ULS combination: T = (M − N z/2)/z with compression, and T = M/z + |N|/2 with uplift. The independent review showed that combining the envelope maximum compression with the maximum moment under-estimated T by about 60% at the governing base. The S3 fixed bases need 6–8 M24 8.8 cast-in bolts with anchor plates (4 at the gable lines), hef 450 mm, 30 mm stiffened plates on 40–50 mm grout.
  • Concrete breakout: without anchor reinforcement the cone utilisation exceeds 1 at most fixed bases and at the braced pinned bases. Designed supplementary reinforcement is therefore mandatory: hairpins around the tension bolts, anchored beyond the cone in both directions. That is why the pads are 0.80 m deep, and it is an inspection hold point. Four M24 bolts are not, by themselves, proof of anchorage.
  • Pads: bottom mesh is the 0.13% minimum or more (≈1,040 mm²/m at 0.80 m, e.g. Y16 @ 175). Top mesh is provided where uplift or base moment causes hogging. Punching includes moment transfer (Veff = V(1 + 1.5M/Vx), BS 8110 3.7.6.2), and one-way shear is checked to SANS 10100. The upward pull-out of the anchor group is resisted by the designed hairpins, not by plain concrete.
  • Wall strip (F2): 0.60 × 0.45 m with ≈75 kg/m³, continuous top and bottom bars lapped into the pads so that the engaged wall acts with each pad.
  • Shear transfer and sliding: two mechanisms, priced separately. (i) Base plate to pad: friction 0.2N under the concurrent compression only; where any uplift combination carries shear, a stub shear key in a grout pocket is used. Bolts in shear through grout are not relied on. (ii) Pad to soil: where the concurrent horizontal force exceeds μN, a downstand key or passive resistance is provided (priced per pad).
  • Fixity: the analysis assumes rigid base fixity. A rotational-spring sensitivity, K = ksLB3/12 halved for partial contact (≈50 MNm/rad for G2, ≈20 MNm/rad for G3), is reported in §15. The subgrade modulus must come from the site investigation.
  • Buoyancy: in G3 a design water level of −1.00 m (0.40 m above the assumed perched level) is applied to all pads founded below it. The uplift resistance uses submerged densities.
  • Durability: steel below FFL encased in C25/30. Holding-down assemblies hot-dip galvanised.

S3's columns are 30% lighter than S1's and avoid S2's imported sections, but its fixed-base foundations cost ≈USD 10,927 more than S1's. The net difference (8k, 2.0%) is smaller than the estimating uncertainty. The headline figures are therefore the P50 values (§15), and the choice between S1 and S3 rests on ground conditions and non-cost factors. Contingency is 10% (design development, no SI) plus scheme risk: S2 +4% (imported sections, knee re-design), S3 +2% (fixed-base anchorage). Erection productivity: 6 columns, 4 posts and 15 bracing pieces per crane day, plus 2 days of girder assembly.

  • Monte Carlo: correlated rate groups, plus independent quantity factors per scheme (steel 0.92–1.00–1.10 for the sizing method; foundations 0.85–1.00–1.25 for the missing SI). P50: S1 429k, S2 441k, S3 421k. P(S3 < S1) = 0.67; P(S3 < S2) = 0.89. S3 against S1 is not decisive on cost alone.
  • Soil (decision threshold): cheapest system G1 S3, G2 S3, G3 S1. In G3 the buoyant, softer ground penalises the large fixed-base pads more than the pinned S1 pads, and S1 becomes cheapest. The SI therefore decides between S1 and S3. Below about 75 kPa allowable, or with high swell potential, a raft or piles would be needed (outside this study).
  • Masonry density 0.7 × 72 kN/m (hollow / lighter units): S1: USD 407k; S2: USD 420k; S3: USD 399k (G2/F2). There is almost no effect, because the construction stage (walls absent) already governs most pads.
  • Wind, opening and fixity cases: see the table above (each case re-sized for the selected column). Structural robustness favours S3. It is the only system that passes partial base fixity, both dominant-opening cases, and transverse SLS at 1.20 kPa. S1 fails both opening cases and transverse SLS at 1.20 kPa. S2 depends strongly on base fixity (55–75 mm with springs) and fails transverse SLS at 1.20 kPa.
  • SLS at 1.20 kPa, longitudinal: all three systems exceed the limit longitudinally. The wall bracing in bays 1 and 5, which is common to all systems, would need a third braced bay per side or heavier members, an estimated +1.5–2.5 t and USD 6–10k for every system. This does not change the ranking. It must be resolved once the design wind is confirmed.
  • Decision threshold, wall construction: with lightweight cladding (h/150) the masonry stiffness criterion no longer governs, and the lightest passing columns are those shown in the "Lightweight cladding" row. The wall type must be fixed before the stability system is frozen.

17. Recommended structural solution

Base case (G1/G2 ground, masonry walls): S3 Hybrid on F2 foundations (indicative member sizes, not for fabrication):
  • 22 columns UC 305x305x97 S355, strong axis normal to the wall, fixed bases (stiffened 30 mm plate, 4–8 M24 8.8 with anchor plates, hef 450 mm, designed hairpins), propped at the eaves.
  • Eaves wind girders both sides, TC plane, 5.4 m deep: diagonals CHS 168.3x5, inner chord CHS 139.7x4.5, eaves struts CHS 168.3x6.3 (purlins not relied on).
  • End-bay roof girders CHS 168.3x5; cross frames CHS 139.7x4.5; bottom-chord bracing CHS 139.7x4.5; ties CHS 88.9x3.2 @ 5.4 m; heel restraint at the gable trusses.
  • 12 gable posts UB 533x210x82 with two rows of restraint struts per gable; gable bracing CHS 193.7x6.3 (two-tier X, 2 panels per gable).
  • Wall bracing bays 1 and 5: X CHS 219.1x8 below +9.90 (in two halves), knees CHS 114.3x5, sill CHS 101.6x3.6.
  • Pads ≈2.3–3.3 m × 0.80 m C25/30 integral with a 0.60 × 0.45 m reinforced wall strip (G2). Re-size after the site investigation.
  • Supporting steel ≈74 t; concrete ≈229 m³; reinforcement ≈8.9 t; cost P50 ≈USD 421k (central 399k).
Alternative to adopt if the SI finds G3-type ground (or if fixed-base anchorage is unattractive to the contractor): S1 Braced, UC 305x305x137 on pinned 4 × M24 bases, the same roof girders and bracing, and smaller pads. P50 ≈USD 429k. S2 is not recommended in any scenario.

17.1 Approval gates

  1. G-A (before design freeze): confirm masonry walls (if they are lightweight cladding, re-run); confirm the code set and the Harare design wind; agree the visibility of the wall bracing.
  2. G-B (before the stability system is fixed): site investigation. Confirm qa, groundwater, swell/collapse potential and subgrade modulus. G1/G2 → S3 + F2. G3 → S1 + F2/F3, or S3 + F3 if the swell potential requires ground beams anyway.
  3. G-C (before BIM implementation): review of this study by the appointed ECZ engineer, then a controlled IFC update per deliverable J.

19. Conclusions

  1. The existing columns, bases, footings and bracing are concept geometry. They do not form a complete or adequate load path for the Option B roof and the masonry walls.
  2. With 12.23 m of masonry spanning to the columns, the column criterion is stiffness (h/300 = 40.8 mm), in both directions, not strength. That moves the optimum away from R2's pinned UC 254 columns.
  3. All three stability systems can be made to work. S2 (moment frames) is the most expensive in every scenario. S3 (hybrid) and S1 (braced) are within the estimating uncertainty of each other (2.0% at G2). S3 is preferred on firm ground for its lighter columns, erection self-stability and transverse stiffness reserve. S1 is preferred on poor or wet ground, where its smaller pinned-base pads are cheaper.
  4. Foundations are governed by uplift and overturning under concurrent actions at the braced bays, the gable posts and the fixed bases. Anchorage, not bending, sets the pad depth. Integrating the pads with a reinforced wall strip is the cheapest arrangement in every case.
  5. The ground and the wall construction are the assumptions that can change the recommendation. Both must be confirmed before the stability system is frozen.
  6. The Option B truss remains appropriate. Its gable top chords, its bottom-chord heels and the bearing bolts need attention in its own detailed design.
  7. The independent review changed the study materially: concurrent anchorage actions, purlin-independent girders, buoyancy, anchorage-led pad depth, a no-restraint robustness test, post restraint and slower erection raised all totals by about 20%, and turned a clear S3 preference into a conditional one (deliverable I).

C. Model limitations

  • Linear elastic 3D frame, small displacements. Webs and bracing pin-ended. Joint flexibility, bolt slip and gusset eccentricities ignored. Masonry not modelled structurally (loads only; minor-axis restraint assumed in the checks).
  • Member checks are in the form of SANS 10162-1, with simplified LTB and the β-factor. Purlins are modelled as axial struts only. Truss member design is not re-checked (R2's scope), except for the collector forces reported.
  • Second order by αcr ≥ 10 (no amplification required). The eigen-analysis is used diagnostically.
  • Results are reliable for comparing and ranking systems and for preliminary sizing. They are not a compliance check. An independent analysis in recognised software is required at detailed design.

E. Independent review

A separate AI reviewer, given the code and outputs but not the author's reasoning, raised 16 objections (2 critical, 8 major). All were addressed by changing the calculations, not the text; the record is deliverable I (review/I_independent_review_record.md). This is an AI-assisted internal challenge, not independent professional engineering certification.
